title: Mysterious object found in South Pacific wasn't Amelia Earhart's plane, Purdue team says
excerpt: A Purdue University-backed expedition found no new clues to Amelia Earhart’s plane on a remote South Pacific island, but researchers uncovered items that could eventually help solve the enduring mystery.
content:
Mysterious object found in South Pacific wasn't Amelia Earhart's plane, Purdue team says

LOUISVILLE, Ky. —

A Purdue University-backed expedition to a remote island in the South Pacific failed to find fresh clues in the search for Amelia Earhart's plane, researchers say.

However, they also said found other items that could still eventually help solve aviation's greatest mystery.

The Taraia Object expedition announced Monday that the mysterious object found on Nikumaroro, was likely a collection of large trees that washed onto the shore.

Researchers first spotted the object in satellite images in 2020.

Its shiny surface led them to investigate whether it could be part of Earhart's plane, which disappeared in 1937.

The team now believes the shine came from a coating of hardened coral sand, not metal from a plane.

"Amelia Earhart's spirit of courage and curiosity drove every step of the search," said Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute.

While researchers did not find Earhart's plane, they uncovered other artifacts.

One was a steel tube about 30 inches long found in the lagoon.

The team plans to study the items further.

The search focused on the theory that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, landed on Nikumaroro after disappearing during their attempted flight around the world.

The island is about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, where they were supposed to land in July 1937.

Although the expedition did not find the plane, Purdue says the search for answers will continue.

"Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown," Schultz said. "That same fire fuels our search. She kept flying, and we will keep searching."
